newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire rebels talk of peace but press on with war.
newsitem.headline: Zaire rebels talk of peace but press on with war.

text.p: Rebels in Zaire said they were prepared for negotiations but they rejected a ceasefire and planned to make new thrusts into the mineral-rich heart of the vast sprawling nation.

Rebel leader Laurent Kabila said the southern and central mining regions of Shaba and Kasai were priorities for his Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo (AFDL), which has already seized about a sixth of Zaire.

"Things are going very well on the military front. We are already halfway into Shaba and in the next week we will be headed further towards Kasai," he told journalists at his base in the eastern border town of Goma.

Kabila said eastern Zaire's largest city of Kisangani would fall despite stiff resistance from ethnic Hutu soldiers of the former Rwandan army, although travellers from Kinsangani reported that it was calm on Saturday.

At the same time the veteran guerrilla said he could accept a five-point United Nations plan as a basis for negotiations, but he rejected the first, and most important, of the five points - a ceasefire before talks.

The rebels, who have been fighting since October to end 31 years of rule by President Mobutu Sese Seko, are in a strong military position after beating back a much-vaunted government counter-offensive.
Spearheaded by ethnic Tutsis, they have suffered no major reverses in the war against Mobutu's ragged army which is backed by foreign mercenaries and Hutu former Rwandan soldiers.
In view of the rebel victories and the retreat of Mobutu's army in a trail of pillage and destruction, more and more Zaireans say they see the rebels as a solution to years of political crisis.
In Kinshasa, soldiers suppressed street demonstrations in favour of negotiations with the Kabila's alliance on Friday.
Anti-government sentiment runs strong in the southern Shaba region, which has several times tried to secede and holds some of the world's richest unexploited reserves of copper and cobalt.
Central Kasai region is the heartland of opposition to Mobutu and home of a long-standing political opponent, Etienne Tshisekedi. It is also home to Zaire's richest company -- the MIBA diamond mines.
Zaire's regions have drifted apart as infrastructure linking them collapsed through years of mismanagement and corruption.
"Why should we want to break our country? Which people want to see the country broken into fragmentation?" asked Kabila, who has always opposed the break-up of Zaire.
Mobutu, who set himself up as the only man who could hold the sprawling nation of over 200 different ethnic groups together, had cancer surgery in Europe in August.
He is now at his villa in the south of France where he has spent most of his time since, returning home to Zaire only twice.
